Abstract
In this study, we conducted research on a deep learning-based blood pressure 
(BP) estimation model suitable for wearable environments. To measure BP while 
wearing a wearable watch, it needs to be considered that computing power for 
signal processing is limited and the input signals are subject to noise interfer-
ence. Therefore, we employed a convolutional neural network (CNN) as the BP 
estimation model and utilized time-series electrocardiogram (ECG) and photop-
lethysmogram (PPG) signals, which are quantifiable in a wearable context. We 
generated periodic input signals and used differential and thresholding meth-
ods to decrease noise in the preprocessing step. We then applied a max-pooling 
technique with filter sizes of 2 × 1 and 5 × 1 within a 3-layer convolutional neural 
network to estimate BP. Our method was trained, validated, and tested using 2.4 
million data samples from 49 patients in the intensive care unit. These samples, 
totaling 3.1 GB were obtained from the publicly accessible MIMIC database. As a 
result of a test with 480,000 data samples, the average root mean square error in 
BP estimation was 3.41, 5.80, and 2.78 mm Hg in the prediction of pulse pressure, 
systolic BP (SBP), and diastolic BP (DBP), respectively. The cumulative error per-
centage less than 5 mm Hg was 68% and 93% for SBP and DBP, respectively. In 
addition, the cumulative error percentage less than 15 mm Hg was 98% and 99% 
for SBP and DBP. Subsequently, we evaluated the impact of changes in input 
signal length (1 cycle vs. 30 s) and the introduction of noise on BP estimation re-
sults. The experimental results revealed that the length of the input signal did 
not significantly affect the performance of CNN-based analysis. When estimating 
BP using noise-added ECG signals, the mean absolute error (MAE) for SBP and 
DBP was 9.72 and 6.67 mm Hg, respectively. Meanwhile, when using noise-added 
PPG signals, the MAE for SBP and DBP was 26.85 and 14.00 mm Hg, respectively. 
Therefore, this study confirmed that using ECG signals rather than PPG signals is 
advantageous for noise reduction in a wearable environment. Besides, short sam-
pling frames without calibration can be effective as input signals. Furthermore, it 
demonstrated that using a model suitable for information extraction rather than 
a specialized deep learning model for sequential data can yield satisfactory results 
in BP estimation.

1 | INTRODUCTION
Over billion individuals worldwide suffer from hyper -
tension, a leading cause of death globally. Frequent 
blood pressure (BP) monitoring is crucial for its manage -
ment (Ma, 2014; Mase, 2011). In recent years, there has 
been growing interest in indirect approaches for predict -
ing BP values based on the pulse transition time (PTT) 
or the pulse arrival time (PAT) (Baek et al., 2009; Ding 
& Zhang, 2019; Ding, Zhang, et  al., 2016; Ding, Zhao, 
et al.,  2016; Gesche et al., 2012; Huynh et al., 2019; Kim 
et al., 2015; Poon & Zhang, 2005; Wang et al., 2018; Wong 
et al., 2009). The PTT is defined as the time difference be -
tween the two measurement points in the arrival time of 
the pulse wave, whereas PAT is the time taken from the 
QRS of the electrocardiogram (ECG) to the time when 
the pulse wave change is observed at the measurement 
site (Smith et al., 1999). PTT or PAT is the reciprocal of 
the pulse wave velocity (PWV), which is proportional to 
BP (Geddes et  al., 1981; Ma et  al.,  2018; Shin & Choi, 
2020), allowing blood pressure to be estimated without 
a cuff. However, arterial features such as elasticity and 
stiffness influence these approaches, necessitating pa-
tient-specific regression equation (Ding, Zhang, et  al., 
2016; Ding, Zhao, et al.,  2016). Furthermore, due to vari-
ations in blood vessel elasticity over time, this approach 
must be calibrated on a regular basis (Chen et al., 2009). 
Moreover, blood pressure features can alter in a matter 
of minutes based on mental state (Hjortskov et al., 2004) 
or external environmental changes (Pickering et  al., 
2005), and the components influencing blood pressure 
are not constant. Several studies have been conducted 
to minimize calibration using a model that considers ar -
terial vascular characteristics due to pressure based on 
the Moens–Korteweg equation (Babbs 2012; Bramwell 
& Hill, 1922) or by assuming that there is a negligible 
change in arterial thickness and diameter with pressure 
variations (Chen et al.,  2009; Choi et al., 2013). However, 
determining the specific unknown parameters based on 
individual vascular diameter, stiffness, and external fac-
tors such as exercise impact and measuring site remains 
unclear (Hickson & McSwiney, 1924; Vlachopoulos 
et  al., 2011). Therefore, more advanced modeling and 
learning techniques are needed to enable accurate anal-
yses and periodic updates.
Several studies have estimated BP using machine 
learning (ML). Previous research based on the deep 
belief network restricted Boltzmann machine (DBN-
RBM) showed inadequate performance owing to intrinsic 
variability and wide limits of agreement (Ruiz-Rodríguez 
et al., 2013). Despite efforts to improve the accuracy of BP 
estimation using PTT and various photoplethysmography 
(PPG) morphological characteristics, clinically significant 
errors still persisted (Li et al., 2014).
Deep learning algorithms have been used to estimate 
BP due to the rapid improvement of GPU computing. 
Previous researchers utilized a convolutional neural 
network (CNN) to analyze oscillometric waveforms or 
envelopes, which indicate pressure oscillations within 
the cuff (Baker, 1990; Baker et  al.,  2022; Forouzanfar 
et al., 2011; Lee & Chang, 2017a, 2017b; Shimazaki et al., 
2019; Zhang et al., 2017). A two-layer feedforward neu-
ral network with a back-propagation training algorithm 
was also introduced to estimate BP (Baker, 1990). In ad-
dition, previous researchers proposed a deep belief net -
work (DBN) and deep neural network (DNN) to analyze 
the nonlinear relationship between feature vectors and 
target values by inputting an oscillometric waveform 
(Lee & Chang, 2017b).
Recent studies have applied end-to-end deep learning 
models to predict BP using various features as shown in 
Table 1. El Hajj et al. attempted to predict BP using PPG 
signals. Various hand-engineered features from the PPG 
signal, such as cardiac period (CP) and diastolic time (DT), 
were extracted and used as input to predict systolic and 
diastolic blood pressure. They examined the performance 
of the multi-linear regression (MLR) and long short-term 
memory (LSTM) models (El Hajj & Kyriacou, 2020). Some 
studies combined PPG and ECG signals to predict BP, using 
heart rate and other parameters, including PTT, as inputs 
for Lasso regression and support vector machine (SVM) 
models (Yang et al.,  2018). Data on the heart rate and a 
variety of other characteristics, including the PTT feature, 
that is believed to be closely connected to blood pressure, 
were gathered and used as inputs to calculate systolic 
and diastolic blood pressures. They assessed the results 
by training Lasso regression and support vector machine 
(SVM) models. Jeong and Lim conducted a study to pre -
dict blood pressure using ECG and PPG signals. However, 
in this study, the original waveform was used without any 
preprocessing to extract the hand-engineered features. 
The input signal is obtained by calculating the morpho -
logical differences between the ECG and PPG signals.
